properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-06: "having somewhat independent reflow2 projects linked allows for requirements from one project to flow naturally to another without a user specifying we need to update package x because package y has a gap that only package x can fix. having reflow2 be able to do this automatically would be great."

THE WORKED EXAMPLE IS THIS REPOSITORY, AND IT WAS ENTIRELY BY HAND. flo2 hit a wall it could not climb from inside itself — a proposed Decision that nothing reported — and the fix had to land in reflow2. What carried it across was a human writing a markdown proposal in the flo2 repo, a human reading it, and an agent re-typing it as reflow2 nodes (chg:flo2-proposal-multi-graph-hosting). NOTHING IN EITHER GRAPH KNEW.

⭐ SHARPENED 2026-08-06 BY A CONCRETE CASE AND A SCALING ARGUMENT THAT CHANGES THE ANSWER. Anthony: "say my brother, who only has read access for reflow2, needs place a requirement upon reflow2 in order for flo2 to properly function... should my brother have the ability to add proposed ideas to reflow2 (write only for proposed, else read only) or should my brother place the external requirement in flo2 and when I open all 3 of my projects, it'll (the agent) see this requirement in the flo2 graph. I'm leaning towards the prior because say projectA (the one being depended upon) is huge and has multiple other projects dependent upon it and don't actually track any of the dependent projects/graphs, then option B may not function... think of it like a Google service is project A...they are not going to load every graph that is dependent upon them."

⭐ THAT ARGUMENT DEFEATS OPTION (C) BELOW, WHICH THIS AGENT HAD RECOMMENDED, AND THE REFUTATION IS RECORDED RATHER THAN THE RECOMMENDATION QUIETLY WITHDRAWN. "The upstream pulls rather than the downstream pushes" rests on the upstream being able to ENUMERATE ITS DEPENDENTS. A widely-depended-on design cannot: it does not know who depends on it, and would not load their graphs if it did. And DISCOVERY OF DEPENDENTS IS ITSELF A PUSH — either the upstream somehow learns of every consumer, or consumers register, and registering is a write. Pull cannot bootstrap itself. It survives only in the SMALL federation case Anthony described earlier (C's owner asking who declares a dependency on C, finding exactly D).

⭐ THE ANALOGY IS AN ISSUE TRACKER, NOT PUB/SUB. Anthony reached for "socket publish/subscribe". Pub/sub is the right shape for the OTHER direction and already exists: the upstream publishes its surface (export_surface, built), consumers mirror it (mirror_surface, built). The REVERSE channel in every real ecosystem is a tracker: you do not get write access to Google's codebase, you file an issue. ANYONE MAY FILE; ONLY MAINTAINERS TRIAGE. That is precisely "write only for proposed, else read only", and it scales because the upstream keeps ONE inbox rather than N graphs.

⭐⭐ IN SYSTEMS-ENGINEERING TERMS THIS IS NOT EXOTIC, IT IS THE NORMAL DIRECTION. flo2 is a CUSTOMER of reflow2; reflow2 is the SUPPLIER. A customer levying a requirement on a supplier is the most ordinary transaction in the discipline. Framing it as "writing into a design you do not own" made an unremarkable act sound like a violation.

⭐⭐ THE VOCABULARY IS ALREADY THERE, WHICH THIS AGENT PREVIOUSLY GOT WRONG BY NOT LOOKING. Checked against describe_schema, a Requirement already carries every field this needs: `source` ("who/what stated it — a user, a regulation, a stakeholder"), `provenance` with an `imported` value, `designation` published/internal so the downstream can mark what it publishes, `status` starting at `proposed` with only the owner's word moving it off (set_requirement_status), and AUTHORED_BY carrying role author/reviewer/approver. A levied requirement is expressible TODAY as: add_requirement (lands proposed) + authored_by <them> role=author + source "<their design>" + provenance imported. NOTHING IN THE SCHEMA NEEDS TO CHANGE.

⭐ AND IT IS ALREADY REPORTABLE, BY WORK MERGED THE SAME DAY. loop_status gained `unsettled_assigned_decisions` (PR #81, 2026-08-06) — a Decision left proposed while carrying an approver edge. The identical shape answers "a proposed Requirement from an external source is waiting on you". THE INBOX IS ALREADY COMPUTABLE; it has never been pointed at this case.

SO WHAT IS MISSING IS TWO THINGS: (1) TRANSPORT — how a node gets from their machine into this graph; (2) ENFORCEMENT — nothing stops a writer doing more than filing, because reflow2 HAS NO AUTHENTICATION and cannot acquire one without becoming a different product.

⭐ TRANSPORT ALREADY EXISTS, AND IT IS **GIT** — NOT ANY ONE PROVIDER.
⚠️ CORRECTED BY ANTHONY, 2026-08-06, and the correction matters because the first version of this node named GitHub: "we can probably use GitHub for this example, but not every project will use GitHub. every project is designed to use a git repo though so other git providers like gitlab can also work."

The mechanism is a BRANCH CARRYING A PROPOSED-STATUS NODE IN THE COMMITTED EXPORT, offered to the owner, who merges it or does not. Every primitive that needs is plain git — a branch, a diff, a merge — and reflow2's own three-way merge driver already operates on the export FILE, provider-agnostic by construction. A hosted forge (GitHub pull request, GitLab merge request, Gitea, Bitbucket) is one CONVENIENT UI over those primitives and supplies the review gate and audit trail for free; NONE OF IT IS REQUIRED. With no forge at all the same exchange works by `git format-patch` and email, `git request-pull`, or a shared bare repo over SSH — which is also what makes it usable where a forge cannot go, including the disconnected case dec:idea-need-to-know-compartments cares about.

THE LOAD-BEARING FACT: dec:multi-writer-architecture (accepted) already made the repo file the unit of exchange, and req:persistence puts the design inside the consumer project. So "the design travels as a file in a git repo" is not a workaround adopted for this feature — it is the architecture, and this transport falls out of it for free. ZERO NEW REFLOW2 CODE.

ITS LIMIT, STATED PLAINLY: it requires the filer to have a clone and a git workflow, which is exactly what flo2's non-technical contributors do not have — so for the HOSTED case flo2's own layer must be the mailbox, and that lands back on req:reflow2-consumable-as-an-image and dec:one-process-many-stores.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN — REORDERED BY THE ARGUMENT ABOVE.

(A) ⭐ ANTHONY'S LEAN: WRITE-ONLY-AT-PROPOSED. A consumer may create nodes at `proposed`, attributed and sourced, and may do nothing else — no accepting, no editing, no deleting. Expressible in today's schema, reportable by today's loop, transportable by plain git, and it scales because the upstream keeps one inbox rather than N graphs. Counter, and it is the honest one: reflow2 cannot enforce it. "Write only for proposed" is a property of WHATEVER HOLDS THE MAILBOX — a forge's branch permissions, a maintainer's judgement, or flo2's own layer — and calling it a reflow2 feature would be the same overclaim dec:idea-need-to-know-compartments warns about.

(B) THE REQUIREMENT STAYS IN THE DOWNSTREAM GRAPH and the upstream owner sees it when they open both. Anthony's own counter is decisive at scale: a heavily-depended-on design will not load its dependents' graphs and does not know who they are. Still fine for the two-brothers case, and it is what the composition machinery already supports with no new anything.

(C) THE UPSTREAM PULLS. Refuted above as a general mechanism. Retained for the small federation case only.

(D) A THIRD, PROGRAM-LEVEL GRAPH holding cross-project intent, with the others as composed children. dec:nested-graphs and cap:derived-completion anticipate the shape. Answers "where does shared intent live" rather than "how does a need travel", and adds a design to maintain.

⚠️ THE PREREQUISITE THAT STILL BOUNDS ALL OF IT: dec:linked-repos-poc was RUN 2026-08-06 and found reflow2 declares NO `required` interface at all, so nothing pairs across any seam. The channel this node is about has no labelled boundary to run along.

⚠️ AND THE CONSTRAINT FROM dec:idea-need-to-know-compartments: an automatic cross-graph write is a channel between compartments, and the safe direction is defined against SENSITIVITY, not against the dependency arrow. Option (A) is materially safer than any automatic flow precisely because a human files it and a human accepts it — the write is deliberate at both ends.



═══ RULED 2026-10-07 BY ANTHONY ═══
Asked "How should a requirement reach a design its sender doesn't own (down to a part, or a customer to a supplier)?", he chose "Write-only-at-proposed" over a program-level design (D) and "stays with the sender" (B). That is option (A), his own August lean.
- ONE MECHANISM, BOTH DIRECTIONS: down to a part it is an allocation; across or up it is a customer's request. Either way it lands at `proposed` in the receiving design, attributed to the sender and naming the sending design, and only the receiving owner moves it.
- THE 08-06 COUNTER, UPDATED: "reflow2 cannot enforce it" was true of a local design then. A design hosted on flo2.io now authenticates every caller and records every write as the caller's own, so a host CAN enforce file-only-at-proposed. That needs a flo2 permission level ("may file proposals") and is a flo2 change, not reflow2's. Locally the transport stays a git branch or PR, and the maintainer is the gate.
- Binding: dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs, ruled the same day (once the receiving owner accepts).
properties.name: OPEN — how does a downstream owner levy a requirement on an upstream design they do not own? (Anthony leans: write-only-at-proposed, carried by git)
properties.rationale:
Captured under the brainstorm skill 2026-08-06, then SHARPENED twice the same day.

⭐ THREE CORRECTIONS TO THIS AGENT ARE PRESERVED IN THE NODE rather than edited away, because each was a different failure worth keeping visible.

(1) Option (C), upstream-pulls, was RECOMMENDED here and is refuted by Anthony's Google-service argument: pull requires enumerating dependents, a widely-used design cannot, and discovery of dependents is itself a push, so pull cannot bootstrap.

(2) This node previously implied the graph could not express a levied requirement. describe_schema shows it already can — `source`, `provenance: imported`, `designation`, `status: proposed` and AUTHORED_BY roles are all present. Same failure dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs corrected on 2026-08-05: asserting an absence from a summary instead of reading the surface. READ THE SCHEMA, NOT THE SUMMARY.

(3) The transport was first written as "a pull request... enforced by GitHub". Anthony corrected it: not every project uses GitHub, but every project uses a git repo. The distinction is not pedantic — coupling reflow2's answer to one vendor's feature would narrow a product whose whole persistence story (req:persistence, dec:multi-writer-architecture) is already vendor-neutral, and would exclude exactly the disconnected and self-hosted environments where the file-and-merge model is the ONLY workable one. The primitives are branch/diff/merge; a forge is a UI over them.

Kept SEPARATE from dec:idea-a-session-holds-several-graphs (ACCESS — which graphs a session can see) because this is AUTHORITY — who may write what, and at which status. The federation node localises this question to each ownership seam; this node is what happens at one.

The reframe worth keeping even if every option here is rejected: this is a CUSTOMER REQUIREMENT LEVIED ON A SUPPLIER, the most ordinary transaction in systems engineering.
